newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Cavallo spatters Argentine chief in graft campaign.
newsitem.headline: Cavallo spatters Argentine chief in graft campaign.

text.p: Former Argentine Economy minister Domingo Cavallo dragged President Carlos Menem's name into his new offensive against corruption Wednesday, saying the Peronist leader must have been aware of some wrongdoing.

But Menem, while admitting he was "hurt" by Cavallo's new allegations against senior cabinet members, refused to get into a fight with the man he sacked last July after doing a widely praised job stabilizing and modernizing the economy.
Cavallo, accusing Interior Minister Carlos Corach and Justice Minister Elias Jassan of manipulating judges to protect corrupt businessmen, said on local radio Wednesday:
"Yesterday they asked me if Menem knows what is going on and I said, 'Yes, he knows what is going on. I myself explained to him how some judges have behaved'."

He also included Menem in his allegations of shady dealings surrounding the murder of a newsman a month ago. Noticias news magazine photographer Jose Luis Cabezas was shot and burnt to a skeleton while covering the summer season at Pinamar, the favorite beach resort of Argentine politicians.

One of the controversial magazine's recent stories, with photos by Cabezas, was on secretive businessman Alfredo Yabran -- a friend of Menem and an enemy of Cavallo, who accuses him of trying to monopolize the postal business for criminal ends.

"From the mayor of Pinamar, (Menem's Chief of Staff Alberto) Kohan, Corach and maybe to some degree the president himself, they all made it their business after the killing of Cabezas to guarantee Yabran didn't do it," said Cavallo.
Yabran has been Cavallo's main target in his outspoken anti-corruption crusade.

After being sacked, he turned on former cabinet colleagues and judges, one of whom is now being investigated by Congress in connection with a huge corruption ring inside Customs, and eventually accused Menem of not taking a strong enough stance against corrupt officials.

"There is no doubt that at different levels in the power structure of Argentina there are people giving protection, and that is very dangerous. I should have gone from the government when I saw it was not firm enough in the fight against the mafia," said Cavallo, using his term for crime rings in government.

The ministers and judges accused by Cavallo have all denied wrongdoing and some of them are suing him. Menem told reporters Wednesday it would be "absurd" for him to sack them before allowing them to refute Cavallo's charges.
Insisting that Cavallo was "totally free" to speak his mind and that there was a "need to extend our investigations to smash these rings of corruption", Menem told reporters:

"I'm not getting into an argument with Cavallo... But I'm not protecting anybody, just supporting my ministers. They can defend themselves and reply to Cavallo, and as long as what he says is not proved, it would be absurd to remove them."
